procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 15, 1964 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 17 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents 2, 3, and 4 filed a revision application before the Bombay High Court after the Additional Sessions Judge held that they could be charged as members of the Editorial Board. The High Court's Single Judge discharged the respondents, finding no good ground for framing a charge against them based on the editor's statement and the newspaper's indication of the editor.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Maharashtra appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the Bombay High Court's order discharging the respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the statement of a co-accused made under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be treated as evidence in favour of other accused persons.

facts: A complaint for a defamatory article was filed against M, the declared editor of a newspaper, and the respondents, who were members of the Editorial Board.
The High Court discharged the respondents, partly because M, in his statement under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), admitted that he alone wrote the article.
The State appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court was wrong to treat M's statement as evidence that exonerated the other accused (the respondents).
law: A statement made by an accused person under Section 342 of the Cr.P.C. is not made under oath.
When an accused makes a statement under Section 342, they are not deposing as a witness.

For a statement by an accused to be considered proper evidence, they must offer in writing to give evidence on their own behalf under the (then) newly amended Section 342-A, which involves taking an oath.
application: The Supreme Court applied the legal principles to the facts, noting that the co-accused M's statement was made under Section 342.
Because M's statement was not made under oath, the Court determined that it was not strictly evidence in the case.
The Court reasoned that while such a statement may be taken into consideration during an inquiry or trial, it cannot be treated as formal evidence in the way a sworn testimony would be.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the statement of a co-accused made under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not strictly evidence and therefore cannot be treated as evidence in favour of other accused persons to exonerate them. The Court held that the High Court was wrong to have done so.

issue.issue_text: Whether a presumption under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, can be raised against members of an Editorial Board, making them responsible for a defamatory article published in a newspaper.

facts: A defamatory article was published in a weekly newspaper named 'Maharashtra'.
A complaint was filed against Sudhakar Gopal Madane, the editor, and three other individuals who were listed as members of the newspaper's Editorial Board.
Madane had filed a formal declaration under the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, stating he was the editor, printer, and publisher.
The specific issue of the newspaper containing the article also printed Madane's name as the editor.
law: The Supreme Court examined Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867.
This section allows for a legal presumption to be made against a person whose name is printed on a newspaper as its editor.
The presumption is that this person was the editor and was responsible for selecting the material published in that issue.
The Act defines an 'editor' as the person who controls the selection of the matter that is published in a newspaper.
application: The Court applied the law to the facts and determined that the presumption under Section 7 could only be raised against Madane.
This was because Madane was the only person who had formally declared himself as the editor and whose name was printed in the newspaper as the editor.

The other respondents were merely listed as members of the 'Editorial Board'. The Court found that the statutory presumption does not extend to members of an Editorial Board who are not declared and printed as the 'editor'.
The Court stated, "the presumption cannot be drawn against the others who had not declared themselves as editors of the newspaper."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the legal presumption under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, applies only to the person who is specifically declared and printed as the 'editor' of the newspaper. It does not extend to other members of an Editorial Board, and therefore, they cannot be held responsible for a defamatory article based on this presumption alone.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the statement of a co-accused made under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be treated as evidence in favour of other accused persons.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was wrong to treat the statement of the co-accused (Madane) under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as evidence that could exonerate the other accused (the respondents).
respondent_arguments: The co-accused's admission under Section 342 that he wrote the defamatory article was a valid basis for discharging the respondents, as it showed they were not involved.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a presumption under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, can be raised against members of an Editorial Board, making them responsible for a defamatory article published in a newspaper.
appellant_arguments: A presumption of responsibility under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act should be raised against the respondents because they were members of the Editorial Board.
respondent_arguments: The presumption of responsibility under Section 7 of the Act only applies to the person who has made a declaration as the editor, printer, and publisher, not to other members of an Editorial Board.

statutes.act_name: Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory presumption of responsibility for published material under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, attaches only to the person who has declared themselves as the editor and whose name is printed as the editor on the newspaper; this presumption cannot be drawn against other individuals, such as members of an editorial board, who are not so named.
obiter: A statement made by an accused under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not strictly evidence, as no oath is administered, but it may be taken into consideration in an inquiry or trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The statutory presumption of responsibility for published material under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, attaches exclusively to the person who has made a formal declaration as the editor, printer, and publisher under the Act. This presumption cannot be extended to other members of an Editorial Board, and in the absence of such a presumption or other evidence, they cannot be charged.
legal_tests_applied: Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867: This section creates a presumption that the person named in a declaration made under the Act is responsible for the selection of the material published in the newspaper.
why_appellant_lost: The presumption under Section 7 of the Press and Registration of Books Act could not be drawn against the respondents because they had not declared themselves as editors of the newspaper; the declaration named only the co-accused, Madane, as the editor, printer, and publisher.

Although the appellant was correct that a co-accused's statement under Section 342 Cr.P.C. is not evidence in favour of other accused, this legal point was insufficient to sustain the case because there was no other evidence to show that the respondents had any concern with the publishing of the article.
The court found that without the applicability of the statutory presumption against the respondents, there was no prima facie case to frame a charge against them.
why_respondent_won: The co-accused, Madane, was the only person shown to be the editor in the formal declaration under Section 5 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, and his name was printed as such in the newspaper.
As a result, the legal presumption of responsibility under Section 7 of the Act attached only to Madane, as the person who had selected the material for publication.
Because the presumption could not be drawn against the respondents, and there was no other evidence of their involvement, the court found their discharge to be proper.
policy_considerations: The court found it fair to exclude the respondents from the case because they had no concern with the publishing of the article in question, reinforcing the principle that criminal liability should not be imposed without evidence of involvement or a specific, applicable statutory presumption.
